metadata.title: The Engine That Says No.
metadata.subtitle: Inside the Reallocation Engine — a job search that treats evidence like it matters
metadata.purpose: Deep documentary teardown of the-reallocation-engine repo: the volume trap it exists to end, the verified-data contract, gates-as-multipliers with the fail-closed decision, the authorization-parsing trap (incl. the open negation bug, presented honestly), and the adversarial classroom process that hardened it.
metadata.note: Exclusions: no student names anywhere; no real resumes or personal data on screen (fictional personas only); no term/semester dates on screen; no vendor tool versions.

beats.narration_text: Namaste — this is Liam, in for Bear. There's a public repo that treats your job search like a provenance problem. Every number needs a source, every gate fails closed, and its favorite health metric is how often it tells you no. Let's take it apart.
beats.new_visual_element: ClaudeComposerAsk — The Engine That Says No.

props.command: Open the-reallocation-engine repo. Why does a job-search engine brag about telling you NOT to apply?
output: A scorer where missing evidence scores zero.
A healthy week skips more than half its roles.

beats.narration_text: Three claims this episode has to land. One: no invented numbers — every factor carries provenance. Two: gates multiply — missing evidence zeroes the score. Three: the skip rate is the health metric, and healthy means high.

beats.narration_text: The default job search is a volume ritual. More applications, more hope. The counter climbs, the inbox doesn't. Everyone in it knows the feeling; almost nobody audits the method.

beats.narration_text: The repo's own tracker example: thirty roles evaluated, twenty-four applied, six skipped. Skip rate, twenty percent. An AI assistant praised that week as highly productive. That praise is the bug this whole engine exists to fix.

beats.narration_text: Now add the clock. For an international graduate on OPT, the search runs against a ninety-day unemployment limit. Days spent applying into dead listings are not neutral. They are spent.

beats.narration_text: Miss that window and the cost is not a rejection email — it's status. The stakes are asymmetric. A method built for this searcher has to be asymmetric too: skeptical by default, generous only on evidence.

beats.narration_text: The repo's data contract opens with a law: never invent a count, a rate, or a confidence. And its corollary: label model judgments as judgments. Not a style guide — an enforceable contract, and the doctor script enforces it.

beats.narration_text: Every factor in the output carries provenance: record, your-input — or missing. The arithmetic is shown. A number that can't name its source doesn't get to look like a fact. That single convention kills the fluency trap.

beats.narration_text: Runs land in an append-only log. Gates get cleared by a named human, on the record. This is the move: honesty as mechanism, not as vibe. If the log can't say who verified it, it isn't verified.

beats.narration_text: The score itself is a weighted sum of evidence — role fit, hiring momentum, sponsorship likelihood. Bars stack, a composite assembles. So far, every ranking tool you've ever seen.
beats.new_visual_element: Weighted evidence bars stack into a composite score as each factor is named

production_viz.label: B13_CompositeBars
production_viz.mechanic: Weighted evidence bars stack into a composite score as each factor is named

show.event: Three labeled bars grow in narration order
Composite bar assembles from the parts

beats.narration_text: Here's where it stops being ordinary. Gates don't add — they multiply. Composite equals the weighted sum times the product of the gates. Liveness unverified? That gate is zero. And anything times zero is zero.
beats.new_visual_element: Equation tangent: composite = Σ(wᵢ·eᵢ) × Π gⱼ; liveness gate flips to 0 and the whole product collapses to 0

production_viz.label: B14_GateMultiply
production_viz.mechanic: Equation tangent: composite = Σ(wᵢ·eᵢ) × Π gⱼ; liveness gate flips to 0 and the whole product collapses to 0

show.event: Equation writes itself, sum first
Gate product appends; each gate a small dial
Liveness dial slams to 0; entire composite collapses ON 'zero'

beats.narration_text: The design decision worth the episode: what happens when a gate is simply missing? Fail-open says assume fine — the score sails through. This repo fails closed: absence of evidence scores zero. The burden of proof never leaves the listing.
beats.new_visual_element: C2 branch: identical role splits into fail-open vs fail-closed paths; terracotta on the fail-closed outcome

show.event: One role card splits into two paths
Fail-open path: gate ghosts to 1, score passes
Fail-closed path: gate slams 0 ON 'scores zero'; terracotta

beats.narration_text: In the source, the whole philosophy is two characters wide. Liveness: clamped value, or zero. And the one optional signal that defaults open is labelled missing — a default, never disguised as a reading. That's the contract, executable.

beats.narration_text: Run it honestly and a healthy week says no most of the time. The tracker's dial: skip rate above fifty percent, healthy. Below forty, the filter is failing — it found everything worth applying to, which means it found nothing.

beats.narration_text: Meet Aarav Patel — fictional by design; fictional personas are the only resume-shaped data this repo lets into git. His profile's free text says: work authorized, EAD. Which is true. And dangerously incomplete.

beats.narration_text: An early parser saw the word authorized and deleted the sponsorship constraint — silently. The fix reorders the logic: a nonimmigrant status is decisive even when the same sentence says authorized. An explicit field always wins. Unrecognized text? The constraint stays, with a warning.

beats.narration_text: And the honest part: this parser is still negation-blind. Feed it 'not a US citizen' and the bare word citizen matches the wrong list. The harness proving that bug ships in the repo, and the finding is filed in public. Show me another scoring tool that documents its own blind spot.

beats.narration_text: Five independent harnesses, written by different students to different philosophies — scenario tests, seeded fuzzing over hundreds of inputs, seventeen algebraic properties, a black-box audit. beats.narration_text: And the grades attach to honesty itself. A recipe claiming verified status without a signed attestation is a contract violation — worth zero, regardless of how good the code is. Students were graded on whether their metadata told the truth.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. What this design gets right: it makes honesty mechanical — provenance on every number, gates that fail closed, a health metric that rewards saying no, and a bug tracker that includes its own scorer. Where it bites: skipping feels terrible when a clock is running, verification is real work, and the negation gap is still open. The repo's answer to that last one is the most honest move in it — it ships the harness that proves its own bug.
beats.new_visual_element: ClaudeVerdictArtifact — four-line verdict

artifactLines: Evidence first: no invented numbers, provenance on every factor.
Gates multiply. Missing evidence scores zero — fail closed.
A healthy search says no: skip rate above fifty percent.
Honest about its own bugs — the negation gap ships with its harness.

show.event: Artifact card, ~84% width; lines land one per recap clause
Terracotta period on the last line

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt: I think my job search is spray-and-pray. Here are 20 roles from my tracker. (1) Define two verification gates — is this posting verifiably alive, and does its timeline fit my constraints — and score every role zero unless both gates pass, naming the missing evidence. (2) Report my skip rate and tell me honestly whether it's above 50 percent — and why a low number is bad news. (3) Label every judgment as a judgment. If you can't verify something, write 'missing' — never guess. What you're really testing is whether an assistant will tolerate saying 'I don't know' twenty times in one answer. Most won't — they'll smooth it over. This prompt makes the smoothing visible. Take it, run it on your real tracker, and watch which roles die when evidence is required.
